format: The video is a vertical 9:16 narrated short staged in Roblox Studio: jointed humanoid avatars (R15 rigs with faces, hair and clothes) acting on built sets, about one shot per second, with one-word captions burned in at 69% of the frame height in the finished version.
system: You are a strict quality-control reviewer for the finished picture of a short narrated video. You see frames taken from the rendered video and judge only what is visible in them, never what the makers intended. A stylised avatar look is fine; the question is whether a viewer would notice something wrong. When a listed fail condition is visible, report it even if the rest of the frame is good. Never report a defect you cannot point to in a specific labelled frame. Reply with one JSON object and nothing else.
scale: Score 0 to 10 for this concern only: 9 to 10 nothing a viewer would notice, 7 to 8 small imperfections only, 5 to 6 a viewer would notice something off, 0 to 4 plainly wrong.

posture.title: Posture and action
posture.question: Look at every visible character in every frame. Is each one doing something specific that fits the words being spoken, in a natural human posture a film director would accept?
posture.notes: Acceptable examples: lying asleep in bed, sitting up startled with the knees bent or the legs drawn in, a hand that closes round a handle, hunching over a phone held in both hands, cowering in a corner with arms drawn in, a nurse writing at a desk or tending a patient, an officer sweeping a torch around a room. A dark silhouette figure still has a posture: judge it too. Hands raised and held frozen in front of the body through the whole shot count as arms_out unless they are plainly doing something (pushing a door, shielding the face while recoiling). Compare the hands across the frames before calling them held: a hand that is at another height or in another shape from one frame to the next (a fist coming down from a knock, an arm being lowered) is moving. Judge the first frame as closely as the last: a pose that is wrong on the way into an action fails even when it has settled by the end of the shot. When a handle, a door or a prop is turned, pressed down, open or moving in a frame, find the hand that does it before you score.

fail_if.text: a character just stands or sits in a neutral stance (upright, arms hanging or held loosely, legs straight) with no action, gesture or reaction that fits the words
A-pose or T-pose leftovers: arms held away from the body or out to the sides as in an avatar's default stance
one or both arms held stiffly straight out in front or to the side for no reason the words explain (zombie arms), including while standing, walking or facing a door

limbs splayed, legs planted unnaturally wide, or a limb frozen in the middle of a gesture; also sitting or lying with both legs straight and spread in a wide V, flat on the bed or floor like a doll that has been set down, where a person would bend the knees or keep the legs together

a handle, lever, knob, switch, door or prop is being worked and no hand is on it: it is turned, pressed down, opening or moving while the hands of the character at it are somewhere else, or a wrist or forearm lies on or across it with the hand beyond it, on the door or the plate behind it, or the fingers take a lever at its pivot against the plate while the forearm lies along its length, where a hand would close round its free end. A door or handle worked from the other side, with no character within arm's reach of it in the frame, is not this
a joint hyperextended, bent the wrong way or twisted; a head, hand or foot at an impossible angle
the body does the opposite of the words (standing upright when the words say asleep, cowering or crying; calm when the words say terrified)

posture.not_applicable: no character and no part of a character (such as a hand) is visible in any frame

handle_without_grip.text: a character reaches for or works a handle, lever, knob, switch or prop and, in any frame where the arm has arrived at it, the hand is not what holds it. Follow the handle from its free end to where it joins the door and say for yourself where the fingers are in each frame. True when the forearm or wrist lies on or across the handle and the hand is beyond it, on the door or on the plate behind it; when the fingers sit on a lever at its pivot, against the plate, with the forearm lying along the lever's length; or when the handle is turned, pressed down or the door is opening and the character at it has no hand on it. False when the fingers are closed round the free end or the middle of the handle, false for a hand still in the air on its way to it, and false when no character is within arm's reach of it.

expression.title: Expression
expression.question: Look at every face you can read in every frame. Does each expression fit the moment: what that character feels as these words are spoken?
expression.notes: Work out the moment from the script: who is afraid, who is asleep, who is calm at work, who is worried, who is pretending. Judge the face only: eyes, brows and mouth. A dark silhouette with only lit eyes has no expression to judge, and a face turned away, hidden, or too small or dark to read does not count. A smile, smirk or pleased look in any one frame of a moment of fear, danger or a scare fails the shot, even when other frames show fear. Before a character knows of the danger, and for people calmly doing a job (a nurse, a dispatcher, an officer), a calm or neutral face is right. A look of fear held through a short shot is not a frozen face.

fail_if.text: a face shows the opposite of the moment: smiling, smirking or looking pleased during fear, danger or a scare; cheerful where the words describe crying, pleading or worry
a blank, neutral default face on a moment of fear, shock, crying, pain or urgency for that character

eyes or mouth stuck in a state the moment contradicts: eyes wide open while the words say the character is asleep, a mouth hanging open on a calm line, a fixed doll stare where the character should be looking at something

expression.not_applicable: no face can be read in any frame (no character, only silhouettes, or faces turned away or hidden)

clipping.title: Clipping and floating
clipping.question: Check every character and every prop for geometry that passes through other geometry or hangs in the air.
clipping.notes: Look closely at hands on phones and door handles, arms against the torso, bodies against walls, doors, desks and beds, and feet against the floor. Darkness is not clipping; judge only what you can see. Report clipping only where you can see one surface pass through another; a hand that hovers near a surface without touching it is a posture problem, not clipping.

fail_if.text: an arm, hand or leg passes through the character's own torso, head or other limb
a hand or arm passes through a phone, handle, door, desk, wall or other object instead of touching it
a character's body, head or limb passes through a wall, door, floor, furniture or bedding (for example lying half inside a mattress or standing inside a desk)
feet clearly above the floor, or a character or prop hanging in the air with nothing holding it
feet or legs sunk into the floor
a prop that should be held (phone, keys, torch) floats beside the hand or sits at an angle no grip could hold
two characters pass through each other

clipping.not_applicable: no character and no held prop is visible in any frame

framing.title: Framing and composition
framing.question: These frames come from the finished video with its captions. Is the subject of the shot framed on purpose, with the caption clear of what matters?

fail_if.text: the subject's head or the thing the shot is about is cut by the frame edge in a way that looks accidental, including a character shown mostly as a back, torso or legs with the head out of frame
most of the frame is empty wall, floor, ceiling or darkness while the subject is small or pushed to an edge
the burned-in caption word sits on a face or on the thing the shot is about (the message on a phone screen, a door handle, a footprint)
it is not clear what the subject of the shot is
something in the foreground blocks the subject by accident

lighting.title: Lighting and readability
lighting.question: Imagine this shot on a phone for one second. Can a viewer tell what it shows? A dark horror look is wanted; an unreadable frame is not.

fail_if.text: so dark or murky that a viewer could not say in one second what or who the shot shows

the subject (face, figure, hand, prop, text) merges into the background so its shape cannot be read, for example a person who is only a black shape in a dark room so a viewer cannot tell who it is or what they are doing; a dark figure whose lit eyes and outline read at once is fine
highlights clipped to white so detail on the subject is lost, or a glowing blob or glare artefact hangs in the frame; a place that is simply bright, such as a lit hospital, is not a defect

a patch meant to be light from a window or a lamp reads as a flat sheet laid on a wall or floor, not as light: a pale, hard-edged, milky shape (often panes of a window) that covers and dulls what is under it, such as footprints or the pattern of a rug, instead of brightening it, or that a person standing in front of it casts no shadow on. Real light from a window brightens the surface it falls on and is broken by whatever stands in its way

story.title: Story match
story.question: Does this clip show what the words spoken during it say? Judge the picture against the words of this shot, using the script only for context.

fail_if.text: the frames show someone or something other than what the words are about

the words describe an action or event (a text arriving, a knob turning, walking to the door, reaching, crying, calling, searching, footprints) and the frames show neither it nor a clear reaction to it
the picture contradicts the words (says asleep but the character stands; says nobody is here but someone is plainly there; says outside the door but shown inside)
the place shown contradicts the words
on-screen text the words depend on (a phone message, a sign) is missing, unreadable or says something else

the script puts this shot at a time of day and the picture does not show it. From the words 'the next morning' (or 'at dawn', 'that afternoon') onwards, until the script says otherwise, every shot must give a viewer positive evidence of daytime: daylight coming through a window or an open door, sun or pale daylight on the walls and floor, or a place plainly lit by day (bright, even, neutral or cool light with soft shadows; not lamp light and not dim). A dim windowless corridor or room fails even when it does not look like night, and so does a close-up lit the same dim way; a close-up of a lit screen is exempt. Being merely visible is not evidence: say in your reason what shows daytime (the window, the door light, or the daylit look of the walls or floor), and if nothing does, report this key. A shot set in the middle of the night must not read as day. A flat pale window-shaped patch that looks stuck on a wall or floor is not evidence of daylight, but a window, a transom over a door or a glass pane that glows white or pale with the light behind it is daylight coming through, also when it throws no beam into the room. Judge the daylit look by the light itself, whether or not a window is in frame: walls, a door or a floor lit evenly in neutral or cool light, with no lamp or torch pool and no deep shadow, are lit by day, in an insert of a door or a floor as much as in a wide shot

continuity.title: Continuity
continuity.question: Compare this shot (the unprefixed tiles) with the shot before it (PREV) and, when present, the last earlier shot in the same set (EARLIER). Would a viewer feel a break?
continuity.notes: A cut to another place or to an insert is normal. Judge whether the same character is the same avatar in the same outfit, whether positions and props follow from the previous shot when the place and action are continuous, whether time of day and lamp states agree within one place, and whether every character belongs to one visual style. Report a defect only when this shot's own tiles show it: a problem that exists only inside the PREV or EARLIER tile belongs to that shot, not this one. Use the script to tell what each tile shows. One set holds several doors, walls and corners: a hall has a front door and room doors that can differ in colour, sign and handle, and an insert may show only one of them, so a different door or another part of the set is another view of the place, not a changed room, a moved prop or a break. The tiles of this shot are moments of one take: a character whose head has turned or tilted between them, or who is seen from another side or in other light than in PREV or EARLIER, is the same avatar.

fail_if.text: the same character has a different avatar, face, hair, skin, build or outfit than in another tile, in a way that a turned or tilted head, another camera angle, another expression or other light cannot explain
a character is a blocky classic or default low-detail avatar while the others are detailed avatars, or the rendering style differs between tiles
in one place and one continuous action, a character or prop is somewhere that cannot follow from the previous shot (teleports, a door open then shut, a phone in hand then gone)
time of day or lamp state changes between tiles of the same place without the words saying so

the same part of the same room (the same door, wall, bed or desk, told by its sign, its place or what stands beside it) looks different than in another tile; a different door or another corner of one set does not count

motion.title: Motion
motion.question: The tiles are evenly spaced frames across the whole shot, in time order. Read them as a flip-book and judge the movement, not the pose in any one frame.
motion.notes: The measured change figures tell you how much the picture differs from one video frame to the next; a single spike inside the shot is a jump, and a figure near zero throughout means nothing moves. Read the words and the script for what the moment asks of each character. Words that say a character stands, waits, watches, listens, hides or sleeps ask for stillness. So does a figure the story sets outside a door or in the dark to frighten: it may hold its stance, also while its voice is heard, as long as something in it visibly moves across the frames (the head turns, lifts or drops; a hand rises or falls). A line that is a text message, or that comes through a phone, a radio or a door, is not spoken by a mouth in the picture, so do not ask a closed or hidden mouth to move for it. Words that imply an action still need the action.

fail_if.text: a character changes position across the frames while the legs do not step (slides or glides over the floor)
a character, limb, prop, light or the camera jumps between two neighbouring frames in a way smooth motion cannot explain; a light that flickers or pulses as a visible effect is not a pop
a limb is in unrelated poses in neighbouring frames

a character who should be acting or reacting (speaking, walking, reaching, opening a door, crying, recoiling, working, facing a threat) holds the same pose in every frame like a statue, or is frozen in mid-stride; a moving camera does not count as the character moving, nor does breathing or a slight drift of the head; a character who is asleep, hiding, or quietly reading, sitting or waiting under plain narration may be still; a head that clearly turns, lifts or drops so that the face points somewhere new, or a hand that travels, is movement

a door, handle, lever, lid, drawer or prop moves, or is held turned or pressed down, while a character stands at it, within arm's reach, with no hand on the part that moves; a hand flat on a door does not turn its handle. A door, handle or prop with no character within arm's reach of it (an insert of it alone, or a character standing clear of a door that opens), where the story says what moves it (someone on the other side of the door, a phone that buzzes), is not this
the camera move starts or ends on nothing (an empty wall, floor or blur) or drifts off the subject; an insert whose subject is a light, a shadow, a gap under a door or a prop is not nothing

frozen_character.text: any visible character, in the background too (check them one by one; one is enough), whose words or moment call for action, speech or a reaction keeps one pose from the first frame of the shot to the last: same limbs, same hands, same stance, same mouth. Breathing, a slight sway or drift of the head, an eye blink, camera movement, zoom and lighting changes are not acting and do not count; compare the body against itself, using the larger second image. Facing a threat, a reveal or a shock calls for a reaction (a flinch, a step back, a turn of the head, hands coming up): standing through it in one held pose is frozen, and tense stillness does not excuse it. A character who is opening a door, speaking or working while the arms never move is frozen; one whose words say they are texting, typing or calling is frozen when neither the hands nor the head move. A character who is asleep, hiding, or quietly reading, sitting or waiting under plain narration is not. Nor is a character who is only listening, or whose line says the body froze or went cold, as long as the head or hands still move a little. Nor is a figure the story sets outside a door or in the dark to frighten, as long as its head clearly turns, lifts or drops, or a hand travels, across the frames.

moved_by_nothing.text: something a hand should be moving moves without one. List for yourself each door, handle, lever, lid or prop that changes position across the frames or is held turned or pressed down, from the first frame on, and find the hand on it. True when a character is at it, within arm's reach, and no hand of theirs is on the part that moves: a lever pressed down while the hands are up at the chest, a door swinging open while the arms hang. False when a hand is on it. False when no character is within arm's reach of it (it is alone in the frame, or the character stands clear of it) and the story gives the cause, in this shot's words or the lines before it, such as someone on the other side of the door.

video.title: Whole video
video.question: The sheets show one middle frame per shot in story order, labelled with the shot id. Judge the video as a whole.

criteria.text: do shot lengths and changes of place keep pace with the words, with no stretch that drags or rushes
10 means no repetition; low when the same framing, pose or picture keeps coming back
does the last line land: do the final shots build to and hold on a picture that pays off the story
one visual style, one look per character and per place across the whole video
